issues.failure_explanation: The paper's own real-spectrum family has rightmost eigenvalue $-1$ and left eigenvector proportional to $(1,a)$. For the fixed initial value $y_0=(1,0)$, the asymptotic condition number is $1+a$ in the infinity norm and $\sqrt{1+a^2}$ in the Euclidean norm. Thus increasing the parameter that makes the matrix highly non-normal can make the real-rightmost asymptotic conditioning arbitrarily bad. The assertion that $|\widehat w^{(1)}\widehat y_0|$ is unrelated to non-normality is therefore false.

failure_location.quote: Regarding the asymptotic well-conditioning of the problem (\ref{due}), we can say that \emph{the non-normality of $A$ has an impact only if $\Lambda_1$ is complex}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Withdraw the claim that non-normality has an impact only in the complex-rightmost case, and state instead that non-normality may affect the normalized left eigenvector and hence $|\widehat w^{(1)}\widehat y_0|$ even for a real rightmost eigenvalue.
issues.overall_effect: The qualitative conclusion AWCnn and related statements attributing large asymptotic condition numbers solely to alignment rather than non-normality are unreliable for real rightmost eigenvalues.
issues.title: False claim that non-normality affects asymptotic conditioning only for complex rightmost eigenvalues
issues.why_classification: The formulas for the condition numbers remain usable, but a substantive qualitative conclusion about the role of non-normality must be weakened; it cannot be preserved by a merely cosmetic correction.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The maxima are determined using $1000$ equally spaced sampling points over the interval $[0,T]$, i.e. with a stepsize $\frac{1}{20}$ of the characteristic time.

If some ratio $\frac{f_j}{f_1}$, $j\in\{2,\ldots,q\}$, is large, or $\Lambda_1$ is complex and $V_1$ is close to 1, cases possible only for $A$ non-normal, \emph{the onset of the asymptotic behavior could be delayed}

This asymptotic behavior also provides information on the non-asymptotic behavior (for all times, not only for long-time). In fact, the strong experimental evidence in Section \ref{NAsy} suggests that, in the vast majority of cases, the maximum values over time $t$   of the condition number $K(t,y_0)$ and its asymptotic behavior $K_\infty(t,y_0)$ share the same order of magnitude.

issues.failure_explanation: The experiments evaluate only 1000 grid points in a finite interval $[0,T]$, whereas the conclusion concerns continuous maxima over all $t\geq0$. The source itself identifies arbitrarily delayed onset mechanisms, so behavior after $T$ is not controlled. It also supplies no bound excluding narrow inter-grid peaks or, in the complex case, larger later oscillatory values. Therefore the reported finite sampled ratios do not establish or provide the claimed direct evidence for the all-time comparison.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either prove tail and inter-grid bounds that reduce the continuous all-time maxima to the sampled computation, or restrict every conclusion to the finite sampled grid and tested ensembles.
issues.overall_effect: The central extrapolation from asymptotic conditioning to conditioning for all times, its use in the non-normal-dynamics discussion, and the concluding 'main result' based on that extrapolation are unsupported beyond the sampled matrices, finite horizon, and discrete grid.
issues.title: Finite-grid experiments do not support the claimed all-time conditioning equivalence
issues.why_classification: The source supplies no complete all-time justification. The only immediate repair is to replace a central all-time and vast-majority conclusion by a much narrower finite-grid empirical observation, causing major loss of advertised scope.
